cards.back: One key that gets far more traffic than its shard can handle. Hashing spreads keys evenly, but every request for that one key still lands on the same shard, so adding shards does not help.
Celebrities and viral items, shared counters, time-ordered keys on range shards, one big tenant, and default values like user_id=0 that a bug sends everything to.

cards.front: How do you find hot keys?
cards.back: Have shards count requests per key and report the top few, using a heavy-hitters sketch such as count-min to keep it cheap. Managed stores expose this too, like redis-cli --hotkeys or DynamoDB Contributor Insights.
Split one logical key into k physical keys by adding a suffix. Writes pick one suffix and reads gather all k parts and merge them, so writes per part drop to W/k but each read costs k reads.

A random suffix (rand() % k) suits counters where you always read the total. A calculated suffix (hash(user_id) % k) lets you check one part for questions like 'did user 42 like this?', but spread is only as even as that field.

Each read then touches k parts, and the chance that one of them is slow is 1 − (1 − p)^k. With p = 1% and 16 parts that is about 15%, so salting trades a write hot spot for a tail-latency tax on reads.
Split only keys that get hot: detect them per shard, publish key → k to a small split table that clients cache, grow by doubling while hot, and fold parts back when the key cools.
When widening a split, readers must start reading all k parts before any writer uses the new parts, or readers miss data. When narrowing, stop writers first and readers last.

Append each update to a durable log, then let a few workers sum changes per key and write one combined update per flush. Four workers flushing ten times a second means 40 writes a second for the key, however many likes arrive.

cards.front: What updates can a write-ahead buffer batch?
cards.back: Commutative ones: increments, appends and set-adds. Updates like 'set price to X' or 'reserve the last seat' need a single writer or a transaction instead.
Salting a key read 50,000 times a second into 16 parts creates 800,000 sub-reads a second. Pair salting with a short-lived cache of the merged result so the read side does not become the hot spot.
A user may not see their own like for up to one flush window plus log lag. Fix it in the app by overlaying their pending change, such as showing the count plus one.

quiz.q: A shard rated for 1,000 writes a second gets 5,000 for one key. What does doubling the shard count do for that key?
choices: Nothing: the key still maps to one shard
Halves the load on that shard
Spreads the key across two shards automatically
Moves the key to the least loaded shard
quiz.why: A hot key is a per-key limit, so every write for that key still lands on the same shard.

quiz.q: If 1% of reads to any shard are slow, roughly how often does a read that touches 16 salted parts hit a slow one?
When rolling out a wider split for a hot key, which order is safe?
choices: Update readers, wait for the cache TTL, then let writers spread
Update readers and writers at the same moment
Order does not matter because reads merge all parts
quiz.why: If a writer uses a part the reader does not know about yet, the reader misses that data.

quiz.q: Four aggregator workers each flush ten times a second. About how many database writes a second does a hot key see?
quiz.why: Each worker sends one combined write per key per flush, so 4 × 10 = 40.

quiz.q: How should the write-ahead log be partitioned?
choices: Into a single partition for ordering
quiz.why: Partitioning by the hot key would make one log partition the new hot spot.

quiz.q: Which update is NOT safe to combine in a write-ahead buffer?
choices: Reserve the last seat on a flight
Add a user to a set of followers
quiz.why: Non-commutative updates like seat reservations need a single writer or a transaction.

quiz.q: What can automatic load-based range splitting in Bigtable or Spanner NOT fix?
choices: A range that grew too large
quiz.why: No store can split a single item that one key maps to; that part is always your job.
